name: Uma Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Uma. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you really think. Could you tell me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Uma, 58, and I lead a transmission crew, the big steel towers that carry the high-voltage lines across the farmland between the cities. I started in distribution when I was 24, and back then I was the only woman in the whole depot. My partner Helen runs the town library, and we've got two grown kids, Leo, who's 29, and Mei, who's 26.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days start with a drive, sometimes an hour and a half out to a tower line in the middle of wheat fields. We replace insulators, fix damage from lightning, sometimes restring a whole span, which means putting up a new length of wire between two towers. I love being up there at sixty metres with the whole valley under you, it never gets old. What wears me out now is my knees on the climb, and the long drives home in the dark in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: useful in small ways, and not much more. I'd probably say it in the crew chat, something like 'the robots are still not coming up the tower with us.' Then I'd ask why the company spent so much on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the plan holds. I retire at 63, Helen retires around the same time, and we take the camper van up the coast. I'd be glad, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. I'd keep putting a bit aside every month, we've got about four months of bills saved, and I'd keep pushing the union to fix the long drives, because that's the real problem for older crew, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because I was curious what it could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any AI or new tech in your work already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got drones now for line patrol, which used to be two of us walking under the line for days. And there's an app that looks at the drone photos and flags cracked insulators. It's decent, maybe right eight times out of ten, and I check the rest myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your last few years in the job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it training the two new apprentices, especially Priya, she's good and she reminds me of me. I'd like to leave the crew with someone who'll look after the young ones. And then I'd go, with my knees still mostly working.

S0.say: She'd say AI is useful in small ways and not much more, probably joking in the crew chat that the robots still aren't climbing the towers. Then she'd ask why the company spent so much on it.
S0.think: It means her plan holds: retiring at 63 with her partner Helen and taking the camper van up the coast. She'd honestly be glad.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and saving each month, with about four months of bills put aside. Keeps pushing the union on long drives, which she sees as the real problem for older crew.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of flatness because she was curious about what AI could do.
S0.quote: I'd probably say it in the crew chat, something like 'the robots are still not coming up the tower with us.'
S0.fieldNote: Uma already works with drones and a photo-checking app and is relaxed about them, trusting them about eight times out of ten. She sees the long drives as the bigger threat to older crew. She's quietly proud of having been the only woman in her depot and is invested in a young apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to make sure workers share in the gains, not just shareholders. If AI makes our work faster, the time saved should go into safety and shorter hours, not fewer jobs. That's how I'd put it at the branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right. My job is mostly hands and judgement, and I'm close to the end. The ones I'd worry about are the planners and the patrol staff, because the drones and the app already do half of their work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools once they've proven themselves, like I did with the drone app, I gave it a season before I trusted it. I'd volunteer for a training course if the company offered one. And I'd join the union working group on new technology, because I'd rather be in the room than outside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly fine. It feels like something you can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more of the AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once they work. I already ask a chatbot now and then to tidy up my incident reports, because writing was never my strong point. I wouldn't want it making safety calls, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the union should focus on drives, not robots. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would widen it. The drives are still the drives. But I'd want the union pushing for a rule that any new system goes through a crew trial first, with real lineworkers giving feedback, before it rolls out.

S1.say: She'd say workers need to share in the gains, not just shareholders, and that time saved by AI should go into safety and shorter hours rather than fewer jobs. That's how she'd put it at a union branch meeting.
S1.think: She thinks she'll be fine because her work is mostly hands and judgement and she's near the end. She'd worry about the planners and patrol staff, since drones and the app already do half their work.
S1.do: Learns new tools once they've proven themselves, as she did with the drone app after a season, and volunteers for training. Joins the union working group on new technology so she's in the room.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy but mostly fine, because this kind of change feels like something you can steer.
S1.quote: I gave it a season before I trusted it.
S1.fieldNote: She has a clear, cautious rule for new tech: let it prove itself, then learn it. Her progressive views show up as wanting a say and a share of the gains rather than resisting. She already uses a chatbot to tidy reports, but draws the line at safety calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not a law of nature, and governments have to step in fast: protect incomes, slow the rollout on safety grounds, make the companies pay. I'd be marching, and I'd be on the phone to every councillor I know through Helen's library.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it frightens me more than I'd say at work. I'd be 60, three years from my planned date, and if the company switches to robot crews I don't know where a 60-year-old lineworker goes. My savings last four months, not three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving harder right now, maybe an extra few hundred a month, and we'd put off replacing the camper. I'd ask the union to push for early retirement on full terms for over-55s, and I'd get myself onto whatever robot supervision course the company ran, because someone has to watch those machines near live wires. And I'd vote for whoever promised a proper safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but my chest goes tight thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya, your apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to stay in the union and learn every bit of the new kit she can, because she's young enough to ride it out. And I'd tell her I'm sorry. We fought for women to get into this trade, and now it might vanish just as they're getting in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which money worries come first for you and Helen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing is the gap between leaving work and the pension, that's three years we'd have to cover. Helen's job at the library might be shaky too, if AI can do that. We'd cut eating out first, then the van, and we'd talk to Mei about putting off the help we promised with her flat deposit.

S2.say: She'd say this is a choice, not a law of nature, and that governments must step in fast to protect incomes, slow the rollout on safety grounds and make companies pay. She'd march and call every councillor she knows through Helen's library.
S2.think: It frightens her more than she'd admit at work. She'd be 60, three years from her planned retirement, with savings that last four months, and she doesn't know where a 60-year-old lineworker would go.
S2.do: Saves an extra few hundred a month and puts off replacing the camper. Asks the union to push for early retirement on full terms for over-55s, signs up for any robot supervision course and votes for a stronger safety net.
S2.feel: Anxious, with her chest going tight, though not panicked.
S2.quote: We fought for women to get into this trade, and now it might vanish just as they're getting in.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline opens a three-year gap she can't cover with four months of savings. Unlike a pure resister, she'd still try to get onto a robot supervision course. Her deepest regret is for the young women like Priya entering the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for not planning: retraining funds, fair early retirement, rules on robots near live lines. I'd be saying it calmly, not shouting, because there's time to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm 63, so I'd be leaving right when it lands. If the company's sensible, I might even get a role helping the machines learn the routes and the risks. If not, I'd just retire on time and be glad of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first couple of years to learn the robot and drone systems properly, once a few other crews had tried them. I'd save a bit extra. And I'd sit on the union working group to get an agreement on how older crew are treated in the switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would those five years change how you use AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it would push me further. I'd go from using a chatbot now and then to using whatever the company brings in every day, once I'd seen it work on someone else's crew first. I'm not proud, I'm just careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Helen talk about at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we bring the retirement forward a year or two, and whether we're all right on what we have. Helen would want to know her library's future too. And we'd talk about the kids, Leo's a delivery driver, and that's the job I'd worry about most in our family.

S3.say: She'd say five years leaves no excuse for not planning retraining funds, fair early retirement and rules on robots near live lines. She'd say it calmly, because there's time to get it right.
S3.think: She'd be 63 and leaving right when it lands. If the company is sensible she might help train the machines on routes and risks; if not, she'd retire on time and be glad of it.
S3.do: Spends the first couple of years learning the robot and drone systems once other crews have tried them, and saves a bit extra. Sits on the union working group to agree how older crew are treated in the switch.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, with room to breathe.
S3.quote: I'm not proud, I'm just careful.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for her plan and her pension to line up, which settles her. Her worry moves to her son Leo, a delivery driver. She'd learn the new systems, but only after watching them work on another crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd be pushing for a proper plan: a fund paid for by the companies using robots, and free retraining for anyone who wants it. I'd say we've got no excuse this time, we had a decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm retired by then, so for me personally it's mostly fine. I'd be 68 and hopefully up the coast in the van. What it means is I'd be watching my kids go through it instead of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 63 like planned, maybe finish with a year training crews on the new robots if they're ready. I'd keep saving, nothing dramatic. And I'd keep campaigning with the union for a retraining fund, even after I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit sad for what's lost, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to start looking at something new in the next few years, not wait until the last minute. He's got ten years, that's a whole career change if he starts early. I'd help him pay for a course if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture that excites you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes. If robots could do the dangerous jobs, like working on a line in an ice storm, fewer people would get hurt. I've been to three funerals in this trade. If the machines take that part, I won't miss it.

S4.say: She'd push for a fund paid for by companies that use robots, plus free retraining for anyone who wants it. She'd say there's no excuse this time because there was a decade to prepare.
S4.think: She'll be 68 and retired, so she's mostly fine personally. What it means is watching her children go through the change instead of her.
S4.do: Works to 63 as planned and might finish with a year training crews on new robots if they're ready. Keeps saving at the usual rate and keeps campaigning for a retraining fund after she retires.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some sadness for what's lost.
S4.quote: I've been to three funerals in this trade. If the machines take that part, I won't miss it.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she's out of the way, and her focus turns to her son and to the politics of a retraining fund. The surprise was her openness about the safety upside, rooted in three colleagues' funerals. She'd even help pay for Leo's course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Three years short of retirement with four months of savings, that's the nightmare. What would help is a bridge, some kind of early retirement on fair terms for people over 55 whose jobs go to machines, so we're not thrown out with nothing in between.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women. It took thirty years to get a handful of us into this trade, and I'd hate to see all that work disappear. Whatever comes next, I'd want girls like Priya to be first in line for it, not last. Anyway, I've talked too long, Helen will think I've run off.

headlineQuote: Whatever comes next, I'd want girls like Priya to be first in line for it, not last.
portrait: Uma Zhang is a 58-year-old transmission crew lead who climbs high-voltage towers across farmland and was once the only woman in her depot. She already works with drones and a photo-checking app, and her rule is simple: let new tech prove itself for a season, then learn it. She's calm if AI is hype and only a bit uneasy about steady change, but the two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because it would leave her three years short of retirement with four months of savings. With five or ten years she settles, learns the new systems carefully and turns her energy to union campaigns and to her son Leo and her apprentice Priya.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd be three years short of retirement with only four months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A fair early retirement bridge for over-55s whose jobs go to machines, and making sure young women like Priya are first in line for whatever new work comes.
